title: Programmable cavity QED with a fiber-integrated atomic array
authors: Stephan Roschinski, Johannes Schabbauer, Franz von Silva-Tarouca, Marvin Holten, Damien Bloch, Julian Léonard
abstract: Strong atom-photon interactions in optical cavities are a key resource for quantum information processing, quantum networking, and the exploration of quantum optical effects. Optical tweezer arrays offer scalable, site-resolved control of neutral atoms, but their integration with high-cooperativity cavity QED systems remains challenging. Here we combine a twelve-site $^{87}$Rb optical tweezer array with a high-cooperativity fiber Fabry-Pérot microcavity. The array is positioned within the cavity mode and individual sites are controlled with subwavelength precision, enabling continuous tuning of the single-atom coupling strength via deterministic displacement through the standing-wave field. For up to five atoms coupled to the cavity, we measure collectively enhanced vacuum Rabi splitting and implement cavity-based non-destructive readout of the number of coupled atoms. These results establish a scalable architecture for cavity-mediated entanglement generation and many-body cavity QED with single-atom control, and they lay the foundation for fiber-integrated quantum network nodes.
summary: This paper reports on the integration of a twelve-site $^{87}	ext{Rb}$ optical tweezer array with a high-cooperativity fiber microcavity to create a programmable cavity QED system. The researchers demonstrated continuous, position-dependent control over atom-photon coupling, enabling both cavity blockade and non-destructive measurement of the number of coupled atoms. This establishes a key building block for scalable quantum network nodes.
main_problem: The primary goal is to develop a scalable, programmable architecture for cavity-mediated entanglement generation and many-body cavity QED, specifically targeting fiber-integrated quantum network nodes.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated programmable control over single-atom and collective atom-photon coupling, enabling non-destructive, state-dependent readout of the number of coupled atoms.
method: The experiment combines a twelve-site $^{87}	ext{Rb}$ optical tweezer array with a high-cooperativity fiber Fabry-Pérot microcavity, allowing precise spatial control over atom-cavity coupling.
model_or_system: The system uses a fiber-integrated cavity coupled to an array of neutral atoms trapped by optical tweezers. The physics is governed by strong atom-photon interactions, leading to cavity blockade and collective coupling scaling ($\sqrt{N}$).
key_observables: Vacuum Rabi splitting, cavity transmission $T(x)$, non-destructive atom-number readout fidelity, and position-dependent coupling strength $g(x)$.
important_parameters: Cooperativity ($\eta=173$), coupling parameters $(g, \kappa, \gamma)$, and the position-dependent coupling $g(x) = g_0 \cos(kx)$.
main_assumptions: The analysis accounts for the finite atomic wavefunction spread ($\sigma_x$) using Monte Carlo methods and uses Bayesian inference for uncertainty quantification.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the schematic setup, position-controlled cavity blockade via transmission modulation, tunable coupling strength via Rabi splitting measurements, and collective enhancement showing $\sqrt{N}$ scaling.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first establishing the physical platform, demonstrating programmable single-atom control (blockade), then extending this to collective coupling measurements, and finally utilizing the collective response for non-destructive atom-number readout.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, highly controllable experimental realization of cavity QED in a scalable, integrated platform, directly addressing the engineering challenges of coupling atomic arrays to photonic circuits for quantum networking.

Two mirrors, fabricated on the end-facets of optical fibers, form a high-finesse optical cavity. Optical tweezers are projected through a microscope objective onto the cavity mode and loaded with 87Rb atoms. A resonant probe beam is coupled into the cavity through one fiber mirror, and the transmitted light is detected on a single-photon counting module through the other. FIG. 2. Position-controlled cavity blockade. (a) Cavity transmission as the tweezer is translated along the cavity axis. The transmission reflects the local atom-photon cou- pling: atoms near field nodes leave the cavity highly trans- missive, whereas atoms near antinodes suppress transmission through enhanced coupling to the cavity mode. The data agree with an exact finite-temperature theory, taking into ac- count atomic zero-point motion and a mean motional occu- pation in the trap of ¯n = 7(1) (solid line). (b) Repeated measurements of the atomic position along the cavity axis show a variation of 1.1% × λ, well below the spatial period λ/2 of the standing-wave mode.

FIG. 3. Programmable atom-photon coupling. (a) Cavity transmission spectra for three representative atomic positions along the standing-wave mode. By translating a single atom through the cavity field, we continuously tune the coupling from the strong-coupling regime at an antinode (i), where a clear vacuum Rabi splitting appears, through intermediate coupling between node and antinode (ii), to weak coupling near a node (iii), where the spectrum approaches that of an empty cavity. Solid lines are fits with the coupling strength as the only free parameter. (b) Extracted coupling strength ver- sus position. The data agree with an exact finite-temperature theory (solid lines).

FIG. 4. Collective enhancement of the coupling. (a) We project a five-site tweezer array with all sites positioned near antinodes and measure the coupling strength of each site in- dividually. The extracted couplings agree within error, es- tablishing the homogeneity of the coupling control. (b) Cav- ity transmission spectra for atom numbers N = 0 −5. As additional tweezers are occupied, the vacuum Rabi splitting increases due to collective enhancement of the atom-cavity coupling.
